brief.topic: Why Common Letters Deserve Shorter Codes

s01: Eight symbols need sixteen bits if every symbol gets two bits.
Can we use fewer without making the message ambiguous?
Our message contains four letter A symbols, two B symbols, one C, and one D.
Give letter A the code zero.
Give B one zero.
Give C one one zero, and D one one one.
Follow the branches.
Every symbol sits at a leaf.
No complete code is the beginning of another, so we know exactly when a symbol ends.
The four letter A symbols now cost four bits.
The two B symbols cost four more.
C and D cost three each.
Fourteen bits altogether, instead of sixteen.
Why give the common symbol the short path?
Swap the lengths for letter A and letter C.
Three extra copies of letter A each pay two extra bits.
The total rises by six.
Short paths are scarce.
Spending them on frequent symbols reduces the weighted cost.
Huffman coding builds such a tree by repeatedly joining the two least frequent groups.
There is a boundary to this saving.
If all four symbols appear equally often, these same lengths average two and a quarter bits.
A fixed two bit code is better.
Compression depends on the pattern in the source, and this count excludes the cost of telling the receiver the codebook.

scenes.narration:
Eight symbols need sixteen bits if every symbol gets two bits. Can we use fewer without making the message ambiguous?

Our message contains four letter A symbols, two B symbols, one C, and one D. Give letter A the code zero. Give B one zero. Give C one one zero, and D one one one.

Follow the branches. Every symbol sits at a leaf. No complete code is the beginning of another, so we know exactly when a symbol ends.

The four letter A symbols now cost four bits. The two B symbols cost four more. C and D cost three each. Fourteen bits altogether, instead of sixteen.

Why give the common symbol the short path? Swap the lengths for letter A and letter C. Three extra copies of letter A each pay two extra bits. The total rises by six.

Short paths are scarce. Spending them on frequent symbols reduces the weighted cost. Huffman coding builds such a tree by repeatedly joining the two least frequent groups.

There is a boundary to this saving. If all four symbols appear equally often, these same lengths average two and a quarter bits. A fixed two bit code is better. Compression depends on the pattern in the source, and this count excludes the cost of telling the receiver the codebook.
